strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: efficient long-context video understanding in multimodal LLMs, where context length and attention cost are major bottlenecks.

Provides a reasonable adaptation of Native Sparse Attention (NSA) to a video-language model by combining compression, selection, and sliding-window branches with learnable gating, while keeping dense text attention via GQA.

Conducts a broad empirical study across long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial understanding benchmarks, with comparisons to multiple training-free token-compression and sparse-attention baselines.

Includes useful ablation studies on branch combinations, context allocation, attention budget, and extrapolation beyond the training context length, supporting the claim that the model can scale to 128K tokens.
Offers additional analyses of gate distributions, inter-head similarities, latency bottlenecks, and attention-sink behavior, which provide insights beyond the headline benchmark numbers.
The writing and organization are generally clear, and the appendix contains detailed training/evaluation settings that help reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core method is largely an application of an existing sparse-attention mechanism (NSA) to video tokens, with modality-specific masking and gating. The paper does not introduce a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The central comparison is not fully fair or controlled: VideoNSA is trained end-to-end on a 216K video instruction subset, while most sparse/compression baselines are training-free. This confounds the effect of sparse attention with the effect of additional supervised training.

Performance improvements are marginal and inconsistent across benchmarks. For example, on VSIBench VideoNSA is slightly below XAttention/MInference/tri-shape, and on multiple benchmarks the gains over training-free sparse baselines are within a few points, with no statistical significance or variance reported.

The paper claims 'leading performance' and 'improved performance' broadly, but the evidence does not consistently support dominance over strong baselines. Several comparisons are ties or small fluctuations, making the practical significance unclear.

Missing trained baselines: the paper would be much stronger with trained token-compression and trained dense/sparse baselines under the same data, compute, and context budgets, isolating whether the gain truly comes from sparse attention.

Some technical descriptions are inconsistent or underspecified. For example, the compression branch is described as using an MLP in the preliminaries but as token averaging in the architecture section; notation in the GQA equations is imprecise; the branch abbreviation SWD/SWA is inconsistent.

It is not fully clear how text-video cross-modal attention is handled. The model applies NSA to vision tokens and GQA to text tokens, then concatenates outputs, but the paper does not rigorously explain whether and how text tokens attend to video tokens during decoding.

Efficiency claims are not fully substantiated: the paper reports branch-level latency analysis but does not provide end-to-end throughput, memory, or wall-clock comparisons against the baselines under identical hardware and implementation conditions.

The attention-sink analysis is interesting but uses a somewhat ad hoc sink definition and is not clearly connected to downstream performance; it remains mostly diagnostic rather than a validated mechanism improving video understanding.

The submission positions itself as the first learnable hardware-aware sparse attention framework for video, but given the incremental nature of the adaptation, this positioning may overstate the contribution.

strengths: Targets an important and timely problem: efficient long-context video understanding with multimodal LLMs.
The hybrid design of applying sparse attention to video tokens while retaining dense GQA for text is sensible and practical.

The paper provides a fairly broad empirical study across long-video, temporal-reasoning, and spatial benchmarks, plus many ablations on branch combinations, context allocation, attention budget, gates, and attention sinks.
Implementation details, training hyperparameters, and model/code links are partially provided, and the authors include reproducibility and ethics statements.
The qualitative analyses of gate distributions, branch latency, and attention-sink behavior are potentially interesting as exploratory diagnostics.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the core mechanism is essentially Native Sparse Attention (NSA) from Yuan et al. (2025b), with a straightforward adaptation to video tokens (e.g., per-frame block size and averaging within blocks). There is no fundamentally new sparse attention algorithm or theoretical insight; the contribution is largely an engineering adaptation plus empirical study.

The main evaluation is confounded and likely unfair. VideoNSA is end-to-end fine-tuned on 216K video QA pairs with 4600 H100 GPU hours, while most sparse-attention and token-compression baselines are evaluated training-free using official configurations. This makes it impossible to attribute the reported gains to the proposed method rather than to the large-scale supervised fine-tuning. Trained sparse-attention baselines under the same data/compute budget are missing.

The reported gains are modest and not consistently state-of-the-art. For example, VideoNSA underperforms Video-XL-2 on LongVideoBench/MLVU (e.g., 60.0/51.8 vs. 61.0/52.2) and is close to or below training-free sparse baselines on several metrics (e.g., VSIBench 36.1 vs. XAttention 36.6). No statistical significance, variance, or multiple-seed results are reported, so small differences may be noise.

There are inconsistent numbers across tables. VideoNSA's LongVideoBench result appears as 60.0, 60.2, and 59.4 in different places; TimeScope appears as 83.7 and 82.7; Tomato appears as 26.5 and 26.2; VSIBench appears as 36.1 and 36.0. These discrepancies are unexplained and reduce confidence in the experimental claims.

Efficiency is claimed but insufficiently demonstrated. The paper emphasizes 3.6% attention budget and near-linear scalability, but does not report end-to-end wall-clock latency, throughput, or memory comparisons against dense FlashAttention and the baselines in the main paper. Finding 5 shows the compression branch is a bottleneck, which undermines the efficiency story without full-model speedup evidence.

The attention-sink analysis is descriptive and not causally tied to performance. The paper claims sparse attention can both 'induce dynamic attention sinks' and 'reduce attention sinks', which is confusing. Threshold-based sink definitions and visualizations alone do not establish a meaningful benefit.

Ablation and scaling studies do not fully isolate the effect of NSA training. For example, Table 2 shows all three branches are needed when trained jointly, but it is unclear whether single-branch models received equivalent tuning. Likewise, comparisons such as Dense-NSA vs. VideoNSA show runtime sparsity helps, but do not compare against other trainable sparse-attention methods under the same recipe.

The training/evaluation setup may introduce train-test mismatch. Training uses filtered LLaVA-Video at 4 fps with 350-550 frames and a 36K token limit, while evaluation uses varied frame rates, token-per-frame settings, and up to 2048 frames; the paper does not adequately analyze robustness to these shifts.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: scaling multimodal video-language models to long video contexts, where dense attention is a key bottleneck.

The proposed hybrid attention design is sensible: preserving standard GQA/dense attention for text while applying NSA-style sparse attention to vision tokens helps maintain instruction-following capability.

The empirical study is broad: evaluations cover long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial understanding across multiple benchmarks, with additional ablations on branch combinations, context scaling, attention budget allocation, gating behavior, and attention sinks.

The paper provides useful and fairly detailed analysis beyond headline accuracy, including scaling to 128K tokens, task-dependent context allocation, and dynamic gate/sink behavior; this gives insight into how sparse attention behaves in video-language models.

Results show consistent improvements over the dense SFT baseline and competitive performance against strong training-free sparse-attention baselines, especially on temporal-reasoning and long-context benchmarks such as Tomato, TimeScope, and LongTimeScope.
Reproducibility effort is relatively strong: training hyperparameters, evaluation settings, code/model links, and an ethics statement are provided.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core mechanism is an adaptation of existing Native Sparse Attention to the video-language setting rather than a fundamentally new sparse-attention method. The main technical contributions are the modality-split hybrid attention and empirical adaptation recipe.

The performance gains are often modest and not uniformly dominant. For example, on VSIBench VideoNSA is slightly below XAttention and MInference, on LongTimeScope it ties MInference, and on LongVideoBench it is only marginally above several training-free sparse baselines. Claims of clearly outperforming existing methods are therefore stronger than the evidence in some cases.

Baseline fairness is not fully resolved. VideoNSA is end-to-end trained on a large 216K video instruction dataset, while most sparse-attention and token-compression baselines are applied training-free or without the same fine-tuning. Dense-SFT helps isolate the effect of training, but the comparison would be stronger if key sparse baselines were also fine-tuned under the same protocol.

Efficiency claims are under-supported. The paper motivates hardware-aware sparsity and reports branch-level latency, but it lacks end-to-end throughput, memory, or wall-clock comparisons against dense attention and the baseline methods. The practical speedup from using only 3.6% of the attention budget is therefore not fully demonstrated.

Some architectural details are potentially imprecise or under-ablated. The paper states that the compression block size equals tokens per frame, but evaluation varies tokens per frame substantially while the block size is fixed at 64, so the frame-level alignment and behavior across settings are not entirely clear.

The paper includes many descriptive findings about gates and attention sinks, but these analyses are somewhat disconnected from a clear practical takeaway or design improvement. They add insight but do not all directly support the central claim.
Potential dataset contamination or overlap between LLaVA-Video-based training data and evaluation benchmarks is not discussed, which is relevant for claims on some video QA benchmarks.

strengths: Adapts Native Sparse Attention (NSA) to video-language models with a hybrid design that uses sparse attention for video tokens and dense GQA for text tokens, trained end-to-end on a 216K video instruction dataset.

Provides a broad empirical evaluation across long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial benchmarks, including comparisons with token-compression and training-free sparse-attention baselines.
Includes useful exploratory analyses: context-length scaling, attention-budget allocation, branch/gating behavior, inference latency, and attention-sink characterization.
Reports improvements over several training-free sparse baselines and token-compression methods on benchmarks such as LongTimeScope, TimeScope, and Tomato.
Identifies practical bottlenecks, such as the compression branch dominating latency and the gap between ideal sparse FLOPs and actual kernel performance.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the method is largely an adaptation of existing NSA to video with hybrid text/video masking, rather than a new sparse attention mechanism, theory, or substantially new architecture.

Evaluation is not fully fair or compute-matched: VideoNSA is fine-tuned end-to-end, while most sparse-attention and token-compression baselines are training-free. No fine-tuned versions of those baselines are provided, so gains may partly reflect additional training rather than the proposed attention design.

Efficiency claims are overstated in the main text: the paper emphasizes using only 3.6% of the attention budget and near-linear scaling, but the appendix reports actual VideoNSA FLOPs are 0.56x FlashAttention (versus 0.24x ideal) due to query-head padding and kernel inefficiencies. The claim of processing over 10,000 frames is not clearly supported by the reported evaluation configurations.

Main results are often marginal or inconsistent: e.g., VSIBench VideoNSA is 36.1 versus MInference 36.5 and XAttention 36.6; 128K scaling improves some benchmarks but degrades MLVU from 51.8 at 64K to 48.7 at 128K. No variance or statistical significance is reported.

Reproducibility and scholarly quality are weakened by missing/placeholder project, code, and model links, as well as clearly corrupted or placeholder references in the bibliography (e.g., nonsensical UML entries and repeated unresolved Li et al. citations).

Technical clarity issues remain: it is not fully specified how text and vision tokens interact under the split attention scheme, and notation is inconsistent (e.g., b/c and s/S in the attention-budget equations). This makes it difficult to verify whether cross-modal attention is preserved.

The attention-sink and gating analyses are mostly descriptive/correlational and are not causally tied to downstream performance. They do not establish that the observed sink behavior is responsible for the reported gains.
Missing controlled ablations: no comparison against trained efficient video LLMs or trained compression/sparse baselines under the same data, compute, and training recipe.
The ethical and bias discussion is generic and does not provide concrete analysis of risks in the video instruction data or model outputs.

strengths: Targets an important problem in long-video understanding and context scaling, with a sensible high-level motivation for sparse attention on video tokens while keeping text attention dense.
Provides an extensive empirical study across multiple long-video, temporal-reasoning, and spatial-understanding benchmarks, plus several scaling and gating analyses.
Shows that an NSA-style sparse attention mechanism can be trained end-to-end for video and can extrapolate to 128K-token contexts with efficiency benefits over dense attention.
Offers useful qualitative analysis of branch roles, gating behavior, and attention sinks, which could inform future work on sparse multimodal attention.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core contribution is largely a direct adaptation of existing Native Sparse Attention to video tokens, with standard dense GQA kept for text. It does not propose a fundamentally new sparse attention algorithm, objective, or theoretical insight.

The claim that VideoNSA is the 'first learnable and hardware-aware sparse attention framework tailored for video understanding' is not convincingly substantiated, and the paper does not adequately distinguish its technical novelty from prior sparse-attention and multimodal efficiency work.

Baseline comparisons are not fully fair: VideoNSA is trained end-to-end on 216K video instruction pairs, while most token-compression and sparse-attention baselines are training-free and not fine-tuned under the same protocol. A properly trained sparse baseline is missing, so the experiments do not isolate the architectural benefit.

Reported numbers are inconsistent across the main paper and appendix. For example, LongVideoBench is reported as 60.0, 59.4, and 60.2 in different places; VSIBench appears as 36.1 and 36.0; similar discrepancies occur in several appendix tables. These inconsistencies undermine confidence in the evaluation.

The claims overstate the actual results. VideoNSA is mostly competitive rather than state-of-the-art: it is outperformed by Video-XL-2 on LongVideoBench and MLVU, and by MInference/XAttention on VSIBench, among others, yet the paper claims it 'significantly advances' video understanding.

The branch-combination ablation is questionable. Single-branch and two-branch variants degrade dramatically relative to the full model (e.g., LongVideoBench 48–49 vs. 60.0), but the paper does not clarify whether all variants were trained with the same data, schedule, and hyperparameters. This makes the ablation hard to interpret.

Implementation details are unclear or inconsistent. For example, the training recipe sets block size s=64, but the architecture section says the block size equals the number of tokens per frame, which varies widely at evaluation time. Such inconsistencies complicate reproducibility and understanding.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix M is speculative and weakly connected to the experiments. The routing-path stability and RoPE discussion does not rigorously explain the observed scaling behavior or justify the method's design choices.

Reproducibility is limited. The code/model links are placeholders, and key details such as exact prompts, data splits, evaluation configurations for baselines, and training of ablated variants are incomplete or scattered.

Writing and presentation quality are uneven: there are many citation/reference errors, malformed references, typos, and organizational issues that make the paper harder to assess. The attention-sink analysis is interesting but not central to validating the main performance claims.

strengths: The paper investigates an important problem: efficient long-video understanding via learnable sparse attention. Adapting NSA to video-language models with modality-specific hybrid attention is a reasonable and timely direction.

Extensive empirical evaluation across long-video, temporal, and spatial benchmarks, with many baselines and ablations. VideoNSA generally improves over the dense base model and several training-free sparse/compression baselines.
The analysis of attention budget allocation, branch gating, and attention sinks provides useful insights into how sparse attention behaves in multimodal video settings.
The paper is mostly clear and includes many implementation details in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core mechanism is largely an application of existing NSA to video, with a text/video attention split; no fundamentally new sparse attention algorithm is proposed.

Evaluation comparisons are not fully fair: VideoNSA is trained end-to-end (4600 H100 hours) while most sparse/compression baselines are training-free. A trained sparse-attention baseline with the same data/compute is missing, and the Dense-SFT baseline alone does not isolate the effect of sparse attention.
Reported results are inconsistent across tables (e.g., LongVideoBench 60.0 vs 59.4/60.2, TimeScope 83.7 vs 82.7, Tomato 26.5 vs 26.2), which undermines confidence in the central claims and margins.

Efficiency claims are not fully supported: actual FLOPs (0.56x dense) and wall-clock latency fall short of the ideal 0.24x, and the claimed near-linear scaling of the compression branch is questionable given that attention over all compressed blocks remains quadratic in sequence length.

Some ablation setups and the exact evaluation configurations are unclear; branch-removal results show unusually large gaps, and it is not always specified whether each variant was trained separately or only masked at inference.
Reproducibility is weakened by missing explicit code/model/project links in the manuscript and by the very high training cost, making independent verification difficult.
